subChunks.title: Behaviour, Health & the Psychology of Illness
subChunks.hookHtml: In 2018, Sir Michael Marmot's global review of health inequalities produced a finding that has since become foundational for health policy: in England, people living in the most deprived communities die, on average, nearly 9 years earlier than those in the most affluent — and spend proportionally far more of their lives in poor health. The gap is not primarily genetic, not primarily about access to hospitals, and not primarily about individual lifestyle choices made in a vacuum. It is produced by the social determinants of health: income, education, employment, housing, social exclusion, and early childhood experience. Understanding this requires psychology — not just medicine. Health psychology is the application of psychological theory and methods to understanding and improving physical health, illness, and healthcare. It asks: Why do people engage in health-damaging behaviours? What makes people adhere to — or abandon — medical treatments? How do psychological factors influence disease onset and recovery? How can interventions change behaviour at scale? It occupies a position at the intersection of clinical psychology, public health, medicine, and social science, and the questions it addresses are among the most consequential in contemporary science.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Biopsychosocial Model

George Engel's (1977) biopsychosocial model proposed that health and illness are determined by the interaction of biological (genetics, physiology, infection), psychological (cognition, emotion, behaviour, stress), and social (socioeconomic status, social support, cultural context) factors. This replaced the purely biomedical model — which treated the body as a biological machine and disease as physical malfunction — with a more complex, multi-causal account.

The biopsychosocial model has become the dominant framework in health psychology and increasingly in medicine. It has practical implications: a patient with chronic back pain who is also depressed, socially isolated, and catastrophising about their pain will require a different treatment approach than a patient with the same physical findings but good social support and adaptive pain beliefs. Treating the biological component alone — with surgery or medication — ignores the predictors of functional outcome that matter most.

Health Behaviour Models

A central preoccupation of health psychology is understanding why people engage in health-relevant behaviours (smoking, physical inactivity, dietary choices, alcohol use, sexual risk behaviour, medication adherence). Several theoretical models have been developed:

Health Belief Model (Rosenstock, 1966): Behaviour is predicted by perceived susceptibility (do I believe I'm at risk?), perceived severity (how serious would the consequences be?), perceived benefits (will the behaviour reduce risk?), perceived barriers (what are the costs of the behaviour?), and cues to action (triggers). Modified by self-efficacy (Bandura): the person's belief in their capacity to perform the behaviour. The HBM predicts screening uptake, vaccination behaviour, and medication adherence reasonably well, but has modest predictive validity — cognition is not the only driver of health behaviour.

Theory of Planned Behaviour (Ajzen, 1991): Intention to perform a behaviour is predicted by attitude toward the behaviour (good/bad evaluation), subjective norms (what important others think I should do), and perceived behavioural control (how easy/hard it is to perform). Intention is the strongest proximal predictor of behaviour, but the intention-behaviour gap is substantial: many people intend to exercise more, eat better, or quit smoking and fail to translate intention into action. Implementation intentions — specific plans for when, where, and how — substantially reduce the gap.

Transtheoretical Model (Prochaska & DiClemente, 1983): Behaviour change is conceptualised as movement through stages — Precontemplation (not aware of need to change), Contemplation (aware, ambivalent), Preparation (planning), Action, Maintenance, and (sometimes) Relapse. Stage-matched interventions are more effective than generic advice. Motivational Interviewing (Miller & Rollnick) is the most evidence-based approach for moving people from precontemplation and contemplation toward action.

Stress, Coping, and Health

The relationship between psychological stress and physical health has been extensively documented. Key pathways:

HPA axis dysregulation    — chronic stress → sustained cortisol elevation
                           → immune suppression, metabolic disruption,
                             cardiovascular risk

Autonomic nervous system  — stress → sympathetic activation → elevated
                           heart rate, blood pressure, inflammation

Behavioural pathways      — stress → increased smoking, alcohol, poor
                           diet, reduced sleep → downstream health risk

Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model of Stress and Coping (1984): Stress is not an objective property of the environment but the product of a transaction between person and environment — specifically, when demands are appraised as exceeding resources. Primary appraisal (is this relevant and threatening?) and secondary appraisal (can I cope?) jointly determine the stress response. Coping strategies are classified as problem-focused (addressing the stressor directly) or emotion-focused (regulating emotional response). Neither is universally superior — effectiveness depends on whether the stressor is controllable.

Social support is among the most robust buffers against stress-related health outcomes. House (1981) identified four types: emotional (empathy, caring), informational (advice, guidance), instrumental (practical help), and appraisal (feedback for self-evaluation). Social isolation is associated with mortality risks comparable to smoking 15 cigarettes a day (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2015).

Psychology of Chronic Illness and Pain

Chronic illness — conditions lasting more than 3 months, not curable by treatment alone (diabetes, heart disease, chronic pain, cancer survivorship) — is the dominant healthcare challenge of the 21st century. Psychological factors play important roles in both illness course and adaptation:

Illness representations (Leventhal's Common Sense Model): Patients construct cognitive and emotional representations of their illness — its identity (what is it?), cause (what caused it?), timeline (how long will it last?), consequences (what will happen?), and cure/control (can I manage it?). These representations predict adherence, help-seeking, and psychological adjustment. Representations that are inaccurate or maladaptive (e.g., 'this is uncontrollable and will destroy my life') are targets for psychological intervention.

Chronic pain psychology: The biopsychosocial model is particularly evident in pain. Fear-avoidance behaviour (avoiding activity due to fear of worsening pain) is a major predictor of disability — often more so than the original injury. Pain catastrophising (magnifying, ruminating, and helplessness) predicts poorer outcomes. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy and Cognitive Behavioural Pain Management programmes have strong evidence for improving functioning and quality of life in chronic pain, even without reducing pain intensity.

Health Inequalities and Social Determinants

Health psychology increasingly engages with structural inequalities. The social determinants of health — income, education, employment, neighbourhood, social exclusion — produce and maintain health gaps that individual-level psychological interventions alone cannot close. Marmot's gradient shows that health improves at every step up the social hierarchy — this is not a 'poor vs. rest' distinction but a gradient affecting everyone. Psychological mediators include: chronic psychosocial stress (status anxiety, loss of control), allostatic load (cumulative biological wear from sustained adversity), health behaviours differentially distributed by socioeconomic position, and differential access to psychological resources (social support, self-efficacy, sense of coherence). Health psychologists work at individual, community, and policy levels — and the most impactful work may be advocacy for structural change rather than individual behaviour change programmes.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen puts a map of London on the screen — a tube map overlaid with life expectancy data. As the Jubilee Line moves from Westminster toward Bermondsey, life expectancy drops by approximately one year per tube stop. 'That's about 12 minutes on the tube,' she says. 'That's the health gradient.'

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: The great temptation in health psychology is to focus on the individual and their choices. Eat better. Exercise more. Manage your stress. And all of those things matter at the margin. But the social determinants research tells us something uncomfortable: the gap in life expectancy between the richest and poorest is produced by conditions that individual behaviour change cannot address — housing, income, employment security, childhood adversity. A health psychologist who only works at the individual level is not wrong, but they are working on a fraction of the problem.

storyBeats.speaker: The intention-behaviour gap
storyBeats.text: A large NHS Stop Smoking Service studied 1,200 smokers who had completed group counselling and wanted to quit. At the end of the programme, 94% reported strong intention to stop smoking. At 12-month follow-up, only 21% had maintained abstinence. The gap between intention and action is the central puzzle of health behaviour change. Implementation intentions research (Gollwitzer, 1999) shows that asking people to specify exactly when, where, and how they will act — 'I will go for a walk on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday mornings at 7am from my front door' — significantly increases follow-through compared to general intention. The plan does not change motivation; it reduces the cognitive effort required to initiate the behaviour at the right moment.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Pain is one of the most instructive examples of the biopsychosocial model in action. Two patients with identical MRI scans showing disc herniation: one is back at work in six weeks, the other has been disabled for two years. What predicts that divergence is not the disc. It's fear-avoidance behaviour, catastrophising, depression, social support, the meaning the person makes of their pain, the nature of their work, and their sense of control. Treating the disc with surgery when the driver is catastrophising and fear is bad medicine — and it's what happens when you ignore the psychological evidence.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
James is a 52-year-old man who has been diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes. His GP has advised him to lose weight, increase physical activity, and monitor his blood glucose daily. After six months, James has not made the recommended lifestyle changes and his blood glucose control has not improved. He tells the practice nurse: 'I know I should do it but I just can't seem to make myself. I've tried before and always failed. I don't really believe this diabetes is that serious anyway — my dad had it and he was fine.' He appears disengaged and ambivalent.

  1. Using Prochaska and DiClemente's Transtheoretical Model, identify James's current stage of change and explain how you reached this conclusion.
  2. Using the Health Belief Model, identify two cognitive barriers to behaviour change that are evident in James's account, and suggest how each might be addressed in a consultation.
  3. What does motivational interviewing (MI) offer as an approach in this consultation, and identify two specific MI principles the nurse could apply with James?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. James's stage: Contemplation (or possibly late Precontemplation). James shows awareness that change is needed ('I know I should do it') but combined with ambivalence and lack of action after six months — which is the hallmark of Contemplation. His statement 'I don't really believe this is that serious' introduces a Precontemplative element: he is minimising the threat, which could indicate he has not fully shifted into genuine Contemplation. On balance, the most accurate staging is early Contemplation — aware of the recommendation but ambivalent about both the severity of his situation and his capability to change. He is not in Preparation (no concrete plans) and clearly not in Action. Stage-appropriate intervention should address his ambivalence rather than providing action-focused information or setting goals — which is appropriate for Preparation/Action but counterproductive in Contemplation where it typically produces resistance.

2. Two HBM barriers: (a) Low perceived severity — James states 'I don't really believe this diabetes is that serious anyway — my dad had it and he was fine.' This reflects a personal illness representation (using his father as a 'positive' reference model) that minimises the consequences of poorly controlled diabetes. A consultation addressing this should use motivational, non-confrontational information: provide personalised risk information (e.g., HbA1c trend, cardiovascular risk calculator specific to James), and explore what James understands about complications and what matters to him (family, activities, mobility) — linking improved control to personally valued outcomes rather than abstract health statistics. (b) Low self-efficacy — 'I've tried before and always failed' reflects low perceived behavioural control/self-efficacy. Prior unsuccessful attempts are being used as evidence that success is impossible, creating a self-fulfilling expectancy of failure. Addressing this involves acknowledging past attempts as valuable information rather than failures, exploring what made previous attempts difficult (identifying specific barriers), and starting with achievable small steps — the first success rebuilds self-efficacy more reliably than ambitious targets that are likely to fail again.

3. Motivational Interviewing offers: MI is particularly suited to ambivalent clients at Contemplation stage — it is a client-centred, directive approach for resolving ambivalence toward behaviour change without direct persuasion or confrontation, which typically increases resistance in ambivalent clients. Two specific MI principles: (a) Reflective listening / rolling with resistance: rather than correcting James's minimisation ('your dad was lucky but...') or providing unsolicited advice (which provokes reactance), the nurse should reflect James's ambivalence back ('So a part of you knows the diabetes needs to be taken seriously, but another part of you isn't quite convinced it's going to be a problem for you personally') — this technique validates both sides of the ambivalence and invites James to articulate the reasons for change in his own words. Change talk (statements in favour of change) from the client is more persuasive than arguments from the practitioner. (b) Developing discrepancy: MI aims to highlight the gap between James's current behaviour and his stated values — without confrontation. The nurse might explore: 'What matters most to you at this stage of your life?' and then, if James identifies things like being active with grandchildren or avoiding the health problems he saw in others, gently draw the connection between current trajectory and those values — allowing James to identify the discrepancy rather than having it pointed out to him.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A health promotion campaign aims to reduce smoking rates in a deprived urban community by distributing leaflets explaining the health risks of smoking and recommending that smokers attend NHS Stop Smoking Services. Critically evaluate the likely effectiveness of this approach, drawing on health behaviour theory and the social determinants of health literature. Aim for 200–250 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The leaflet campaign reflects an information-deficit model of behaviour change: if people knew the risks, they would stop. This model is both theoretically and empirically weak. Awareness of smoking health risks is near-universal — virtually all smokers know smoking damages their health. The gap is not informational. The Health Belief Model would predict that information alone fails when perceived barriers are high (addiction, social norms, stress relief function of smoking) and self-efficacy is low — both conditions prevalent in deprived communities.

The social determinants literature is particularly challenging here. In deprived communities, smoking prevalence is higher not because people are less informed or less rational but because smoking performs specific functions: stress regulation in contexts of chronic psychosocial stress, social bonding in communities where tobacco remains normative, and one of few available sources of pleasure and autonomy in constrained lives. A leaflet addressing none of these functions will not shift behaviour.

Transtheoretical Model analysis suggests most smokers in any community are in Precontemplation or Contemplation — not ready for an action-focused referral to Stop Smoking Services. Stage-matched approaches — brief motivational conversations, normalising ambivalence, building self-efficacy through small steps — are more effective than referral services that require Preparation-stage readiness.

A more effective approach would combine: brief advice with motivational conversation from trusted primary care contacts; easy access to NRT (prescriptions, not leaflets); addressing the stress context (employment, housing); and community-level norm change. Information provision is not harmful — but relying on it as the primary mechanism is not evidence-based.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why knowing something is bad for your health — like smoking or not exercising — doesn't automatically make people stop doing it. What do psychologists think is actually going on?

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Engel's (1977) framework replacing the purely biomedical model: health and illness result from the interaction of biological, psychological, and social factors. Now the dominant paradigm in health psychology and increasingly in medicine and public health.

Gollwitzer's (1999) technique for closing the intention-behaviour gap: forming specific 'if-then' plans specifying when, where, and how a behaviour will be performed. Significantly increases follow-through compared to general intention alone across health behaviours.

A model of chronic pain disability: catastrophic interpretation of pain → fear of movement → avoidance behaviour → deconditioning and disability, with pain becoming increasingly associated with threat. Central to understanding why some people with physical injuries develop chronic disability while others recover.

McEwen's (1998) concept of cumulative biological wear and tear produced by chronic stress — measured across multiple physiological systems (HPA axis, cardiovascular, immune, metabolic). Higher allostatic load (more wear) predicts morbidity and mortality and is more prevalent in socioeconomically disadvantaged populations.

questions.questionHtml: In Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, what is 'secondary appraisal'?
options: The initial judgment about whether a situation is threatening or relevant
The evaluation of available coping resources and whether one can manage the demands of the situation
The reappraisal of a situation after coping has been attempted
Social comparison with others facing similar stressors
questions.correctAnswer: The evaluation of available coping resources and whether one can manage the demands of the situation
questions.explanationHtml: In Lazarus and Folkman's model, stress is a transaction between person and environment. Primary appraisal determines whether a situation is relevant and potentially threatening (is this stressful?). Secondary appraisal evaluates what can be done — the person's assessment of available coping resources, options for response, and their perceived capacity to manage the demands. It is the interaction of primary and secondary appraisal that determines the stress response: a demanding situation is only stressful when demands are appraised as exceeding available coping resources. This explains why the same event produces very different stress responses in different people — their appraisals differ.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: Research consistently shows that the most effective way to change health behaviours like smoking or physical inactivity is to provide clear information about the health risks involved.
questions.explanationHtml: False. The information-deficit model — that behaviour change follows from knowledge of risk — is not well-supported by evidence. Smoking cessation research shows near-universal awareness of health risks among smokers; information provision is not the limiting factor. Health behaviour models (Health Belief Model, Theory of Planned Behaviour, Transtheoretical Model) all identify additional determinants beyond risk knowledge: perceived self-efficacy, social norms, perceived barriers, stage of readiness, and structural context. The intention-behaviour gap further demonstrates that even when people intend to change, they often fail to do so without additional support (e.g., implementation intentions, social support, reduced barriers). Information campaigns have weak evidence for producing sustained behaviour change, particularly in populations facing significant structural and social barriers.

questions.questionHtml: A health psychologist is designing an intervention to increase physical activity in adults with chronic pain who fear that exercise will worsen their condition. Which approach has the strongest evidence for this population?
options: Providing detailed information about the health benefits of exercise and debunking the idea that exercise causes harm
A graded activity programme combined with Cognitive Behavioural Pain Management addressing fear-avoidance beliefs and pain catastrophising
Recommending complete rest until pain is better controlled by medication
Referring to a physiotherapist for passive treatment to reduce pain before activity is introduced
questions.correctAnswer: A graded activity programme combined with Cognitive Behavioural Pain Management addressing fear-avoidance beliefs and pain catastrophising
questions.explanationHtml: For chronic pain patients with fear-avoidance behaviour, the most evidence-based approach combines graded physical activity (gradually increasing movement and function within the patient's tolerance, based on pacing rather than pain signals as a guide) with cognitive-behavioural work targeting fear-avoidance beliefs, catastrophising, and the patient's illness representations. This approach has strong RCT evidence for improving functioning and quality of life even without reducing pain intensity. Information provision alone (option A) has limited effectiveness when fear and catastrophising are the primary barriers — it is not sufficient to correct the belief that exercise causes harm because that belief is maintained by avoidance behaviour, not lack of information. Complete rest (option C) increases disability and deconditioning. Passive physiotherapy without psychological components addresses neither the fear-avoidance beliefs nor the activity pattern that maintains disability.
